sec: Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Mountain Roads · ¶1
text: If two vehicles meet on a steep narrow road and neither vehicle can pass, the vehicle facing uphill has the right-of-way. The vehicle facing downhill has more control when backing up the hill. The vehicle facing downhill should back up until the vehicle going uphill can pass.

page: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Turning · ¶1
text: When a vehicle turns, the rear wheels follow a shorter path than the front wheels. The longer the vehicle, the greater the difference in the length of the turning path. This is why large vehicles and truck drivers must often swing wide to complete a turn. When you follow a large vehicle, look at its turn signals before you start to pass. It may appear to be turning one direction but instead is swinging wide in the opposite direction in order to turn.
why: large vehicles: look at turn signals before you start to pass

page: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · ¶1
text: Large vehicles and trucks are not as easy to maneuver as passenger vehicles. On a divided highway with four or more traffic lanes in one direction, they may be driven in the two lanes farthest to the right. When driving near large vehicles and trucks, do not:
why: context: list lead 'When driving near large vehicles and trucks, do not:'

page: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 2
text: Drive next to them longer than you need to. Always pass a large vehicle on the left side. After you pass the large vehicle or truck, move ahead of it. Driving alongside a large vehicle makes it hard for the driver to avoid dangers in the road.
why: large vehicles: do not drive alongside; always pass on the left; move ahead after passing

page: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued)
sec: Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶1

text: Motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicle drivers. To safely share the road with motorcyclists:

page: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued)
sec: Choose Between Hazards · ¶1
text: Sometimes dangers will be on both sides of the road at the same time. For example, parked cars to the right and oncoming cars to the left.
why: context: hazards on both sides of the road (example lead)

page: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued)
sec: Choose Between Hazards · ¶2
text: If one danger is greater than the other, give more space to the most dangerous situation. Suppose you are on a two-lane road with an oncoming vehicle to the left and a bicyclist ahead to your right. Instead of driving between the vehicle and the bicyclist, take one danger at a time. Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass. When the vehicle has passed, move to the left to allow plenty of space (at least three feet) to pass the bicyclist. If there is a steady flow of oncoming vehicles, use as much of the left lane as you safely can to pass the bicyclist.
why: oncoming vehicle and bicyclist: take one danger at a time, at least three feet to pass the bicyclist

sec: Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶2
text: If you see a vehicle’s emergency flashers ahead, slow down. There may be a collision or other road emergency. Pass carefully.

page: Section 14: Glossary
sec: Intro · row 6
text: Three-second rule | A driving rule that helps you estimate how closely you should follow other vehicles. When the vehicle in front of you passes a certain point, such as a sign, count three seconds. If you pass the same point before you finish counting, you are following too closely.
why: three-second rule: a vehicle passes a certain point ('pass' = go by)
